rows.description: A child is satisfied with a simple toy and a good afternoon and does not compare it with others. Contentment at this age is fragile against advertisements and peers' possessions.
A teenager who was fine with their phone or marks feels lacking after seeing friends' posts. Constant comparison manufactures dissatisfaction from nothing that has actually changed.
A child rests quietly in a parent's lap and breathes slowly. Early serenity is borrowed from a calm adult, and the child stores it as a felt memory of safety.
A student before an interview or a viva feels nerves yet stays steady, having accepted that not everything is in their control. Calm here is a practised stance, not the absence of fear.
A child stares wide-eyed at a rainbow, an ant colony or thunder and asks endless questions. Awe at this age is simple, bodily and contagious, and adults who share the gaze deepen it.
A child looking at a night sky or a huge river feels small yet strangely happy. Awe expands the sense of the world and, oddly, softens self-focus.
A teenager moved by a scientist, a mountain, a devotional song or a stranger's kindness feels lifted beyond daily worries. Awe can arise from moral beauty as much as from scenery.

rows.subtype: Toddler recharging after a big day [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler after an outing wants quiet, a familiar toy and closeness, and may fall apart if pushed to do more. Rest is part of how small children absorb what they have experienced.

rows.subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager in a schedule of school, tuition and activities has no space to rest and feels flat, resentful or anxious. Building free time into the week is not wasted, since the mind consolidates and recovers in it.
A young adult who feels lazy whenever not productive finds rest empty and anxious. Learning that recovery makes later work better allows genuine rest without guilt.

rows.subtype: Laughing at a fall or a shock [Mismatch]
rows.description: A toddler may laugh after a bump or a scare, while looking to a parent for a reaction. It can be relief, confusion or imitation, not callousness; a calm response shows the child whether the moment was safe.

A teenager laughs when embarrassed, scared, being scolded or hearing bad news. It signals stress release, not enjoyment or disrespect; reading it as mockery causes conflict, while a gentle check on feelings helps.

rows.subtype: Laughing through hurt and gallows humour [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young adult laughs about stress, a mistake or a hard time as a coping tool. It can show resilience but sometimes hides pain; a friend who listens without assuming can tell which by gently asking how they really are.
A teenager who owns a mistake with a plain sorry finds that relationships recover faster than through defensiveness. Taking responsibility is strength, and it does not mean accepting all blame.
A person listens kindly, then asks what the other wants to do about the situation and stays firm about their own limits. This respects pain without accepting blame that is not theirs.
